extracted.intended_audience: Government departments and other public bodies (policy makers)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for when, with whom and how government departments and public bodies should consult stakeholders while developing policy and legislation. Emphasises proportionality, accessibility, transparency and practical procedures for running consultations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: The governing principle is proportionality of the type and scale of consultation to the potential impacts of the proposal or decision being taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation design (scope, length, methods, level of detail) should match the likely impact and complexity of the proposal. Aim for real engagement rather than merely following bureaucratic process; decisions on whether and how to consult should depend on the wider scheme of engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin engagement early
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement should begin early in policy development when the policy is still under consideration and views can genuinely be taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are several stages of policy development; use different ways of engaging at different stages. Make the Government’s evidence base available at an early stage to enable contestability and challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear objectives for consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: The objectives of any consultation should be clear, and will depend to a great extent on the type of issue and the stage in the policy-making process – from gathering new ideas to testing options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the purpose of the consultation and the stage of development the policy has reached. Be explicit about what aspects are open to change and what decisions have already been taken to avoid creating unrealistic expectations and to increase usefulness of responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and consult the full range of stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy makers should be able to demonstrate that they have considered who needs to be consulted and ensure that the consultation captures the full range of stakeholders affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the diversity of interested parties and target those with a substantial interest. Where the policy will affect hard-to-reach or vulnerable groups, take necessary actions to engage effectively with these groups and consider their capacity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate and realistic timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeframes for consultation should be proportionate and realistic to allow stakeholders sufficient time to provide a considered response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amount of time depends on nature and impact of the proposal (e.g. complexity, diversity of stakeholders, external events). Typical consultations might vary between two and 12 weeks; where appropriate conduct 12-week formal written consultations, with clear explanations and rationale for shorter time-frames. Consider holiday periods and the capacity of groups being consulted; decide length case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make information useful and accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Information provided to stakeholders should be easy to comprehend – in an easily understandable format, use plain language and clarify the key issues, particularly where the consultation deals with complex subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disseminate and present information in ways likely to be accessible and useful to interested stakeholders. Post relevant documentation online to enhance accessibility and opportunities for reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate consultation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of the form of consultation will largely depend on: the issues under consideration, who needs to be consulted, and the available time and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider modern communications technologies and more informal forms (email, web-based forums, public meetings, working groups, focus groups, surveys) rather than always reverting to traditional written consultations. Avoid imposing disproportionate cost on government or stakeholders when selecting methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and feedback on responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the consultation process should be clearly stated and policy makers should explain what responses they have received and how these have been used in formulating the policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate the number of responses received. Consultation responses should usually be published within 12 weeks of the consultation closing; where not published within 12 weeks, provide a brief statement explaining why. Make clear, at least broadly, future plans for engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: House consultations on GOV.UK
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure transparency and consistency of approach, all consultations should be housed on the Government’s single web platform (GOV.UK).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the central platform to post relevant documents and ensure consistency, discoverability and accessibility of consultation materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to consulting
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be circumstances where formal consultation is not appropriate (for example, where the measure is necessary to deal with a court judgment or where adequate consultation has taken place at an earlier stage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on a case-by-case basis whether consultation is required. For minor or technical amendments or when previous adequate engagement has occurred, formal consultation may not be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer/detailed consultation when vulnerable groups affected
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer and more detailed consultation will be needed in situations where smaller, more vulnerable organisations such as small charities could be affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect obligations such as the Compact between government and the voluntary and community sector; take extra steps to ensure meaningful engagement with groups lacking capacity or resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid consultation during elections where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation exercises should not generally be launched during local or national election periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exceptional circumstances make a consultation essential during an election period (e.g. safeguarding public health), seek advice from the Propriety and Ethics team in the Cabinet Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior-level oversight and collective ministerial agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments should be clear how they have come to the decision to consult, and senior officials and ministers should be sighted on the considerations taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek collective ministerial agreement before any public engagement that might be seen as committing the Government to a particular approach. Ensure supporting documents for formal consultations are cleared collectively; where using informal methods consider at what point collective agreement should be sought. The Cabinet Secretariat can advise on particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance is not legally binding; comply with statutory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: This guidance does not have legal force and does not prevail over statutory or mandatory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with any laws that impose consultation obligations for certain issues and other legal requirements that may affect consultation exercises (for example confidentiality or equality obligations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of costs and burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy-makers should avoid disproportionate cost to the Government or the stakeholders concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the value of engagement against cost and administrative burden; select methods and scope that are proportionate to benefits and stakeholder capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make evidence available to enable contestability
rubrics_metrics.description: Every effort should be made to make available the Government’s evidence base at an early stage to enable contestability and challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing the evidence base increases transparency, allows external scrutiny, and improves the quality of policy making by bringing in expertise and alternative perspectives.
